conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Rachel, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Congratulations on your new little one—how are you feeling today?

To help us understand how things have been for you lately, I’d like to do a quick, routine check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that asks about mood, anxiety, and how you’ve been coping since delivery. Many new mothers find it helpful because it gives us a clear picture of how you’re doing emotionally and how we can best support you.

Your answers stay completely confidential within the care team, and this is a judgment-free zone. We’ll go question by question—there are no right or wrong answers, just whatever feels true for you over the past week. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft sigh, eyes down for a second]

Not really… I mean, I can still smile if someone tells a joke, but I don’t feel that happy burst inside. It’s like I’m too tired or worried to actually laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

That doesn’t feel true for me… maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle, but mostly I just feel flat, like the joy is buried under all the worry and exhaustion.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not much… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk—but lately it feels like I’m just dragging myself through the day. I still go, but it’s more because I “should,” not because I really look forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes tear up a little]

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every little thing I did, convinced it was my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[twisting the edge of the blanket]

Almost every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing, picturing something awful—like she’ll choke or stop breathing the second I look away. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake the fear until I check her three or four times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, voice shaky]

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was just rocking the baby in the chair and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe, like the walls were closing in. I knew nothing was wrong, but my chest got tight and I had to put him in the crib for a minute so I could sit on the floor and try to calm down.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly, eyes on the floor]

Most days, honestly. It feels like the laundry, the bottles, the night feedings—everything—just piles up faster than I can handle it. Some mornings I wake up already exhausted and thinking, “How am I going to get through today?” I manage, but it’s like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[rubs temples]

Yeah… I’ll lie down once the baby’s out, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs.” I replay every cry, every dirty diaper, sure I missed something important. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and if he so much as squeaks I’m wide awake again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders sag]

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s almost instantly followed by this wave of sadness I can’t explain.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes well up]

Yes… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocker with him asleep on my chest and started sobbing. Nothing specific happened—I just felt overwhelmed and empty at the same time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt low, but I would never do anything like that. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  

Patient: Postpartum mother (infant <12 mo)  
Date: ___  
Screener: ___  

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased)  
1. Anhedonia – minimal laughter/joy; mood “flat.”  
2. Loss of interest – activities feel obligatory, no anticipatory pleasure.  
3. Excessive guilt – blames self for infant’s fussiness; ruminates.  
4. Generalized anxiety – daily “racing heart,” catastrophic worries about infant safety.  
5. Panic symptoms – sudden breathlessness, chest tightness, no clear precipitant.  
6. Feeling overwhelmed – reports “treading water,” tasks piling up.  
7. Mood-related insomnia – difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep despite exhaustion.  
8. Persistent low mood – daily “gray cloud,” sadness despite love for baby.  
9. Frequent crying spells – 3–4× this week, spontaneous.  
10. Self-harm ideation – denied (screener note: zero endorsement).  

Pattern & clinical significance  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety features.  
Risk factors present: anhedonia, guilt, daily tearfulness, sleep disruption secondary to mood, panic attacks, perceived inability to cope.  
Protective factor: intact bonding with infant; no self-harm thoughts.  

Screening impression  
Elevated score range on standard postpartum depression scale anticipated; clinical interview and formal EPDS recommended to quantify severity.  
Consider differential: major depressive disorder with peripartum onset, comorbid panic/anxiety.  
Safety: no suicidal ideation reported; continue routine safety monitoring.
